title: WHEN DESIRE STOPS SEEING A SOUL
paragraphs:
WHEN DESIRE STOPS SEEING A SOUL
You can desire someone’s body so intensely that you slowly forget there is a soul living inside it.
There is a kind of desire that looks like love from across the room.
It knows exactly what makes the heart race.
But there is one terrifying question it may never ask:
What is good for your soul?
Because you can crave someone's presence without cherishing the person.
You can be fascinated by someone's body while remaining indifferent to their eternity.
You can call something “chemistry” when, beneath the beautiful words, what you really mean is:
I want what you make me feel.
That is where desire becomes dangerous.
Not because sexual desire itself is dirty.

Christianity does not teach that the human body is disgusting or that attraction itself is sinful. God created humanity embodied. Scripture can speak beautifully and positively about marital desire. The problem begins when desire stops asking how to love another person before God and starts asking only how another person can satisfy me.
Then a person quietly becomes a product.
A body becomes something to consume.
A photograph becomes something to use.
And intimacy becomes consumption disguised as connection.
Maybe your Bible is beside your bed while your phone contains a completely different version of you.
Maybe there is someone you keep thinking about whom you have never even touched.
Maybe there are messages you would panic to see projected onto the church wall.
Maybe pornography has trained your eyes to undress people your mouth would politely greet.
Maybe you have learned to call lust “admiration” because the softer word hurts less.
Or maybe somebody did this to you.
Maybe someone told you that you were beautiful when what they really meant was that you were useful to their appetite.
Maybe they wanted your body but never wanted the responsibility of protecting your heart.
Maybe they promised permanence until they received access.
And you were left staring at a screen wondering how somebody who once made you feel so wanted could suddenly make you feel so disposable.
If that happened to you, understand something Scripture has been telling humanity for centuries:
Being desired is not the same thing as being loved.
Love asks, “How can I seek your good?”
Lust can be willing to damage tomorrow for pleasure tonight.
Christlike love refuses to treat another human being as an instrument for gratification.
And Jesus takes this far deeper than outward behavior.

In Matthew 5:28, Christ confronts the desire of the heart. The Greek expression includes πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn, speaking of looking toward a woman with the purpose of lusting after her.
Into the secret room where nobody applauds your holiness because nobody knows what you are thinking.
Because Jesus is not merely trying to prevent scandal.

The Greek verb connected with desire here, ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, can refer to strong desire; context determines whether that desire is right or corrupt. So the biblical answer is not the annihilation of every human desire.
It is the redemption of desire.
Christ does not simply ask, “Did you touch?”
Did you see an image or a person?
Did you see curves, muscles, skin, attention, validation, fantasy...
or did you remember that you were looking at someone made in the image of God?
That person has wounds you cannot see.
That person has someone who once held them as a baby.
That person will someday stand before God.
Not a body placed on earth to medicate your loneliness.
And suddenly the issue becomes much bigger than sex.
Paul writes with almost shocking directness in 1 Corinthians 6:18:
Paul does not say negotiate with it.
Study how close you can stand to it.
Keep it in your private messages.
See how much temptation you can tolerate before crossing some imaginary Christian line.
Because biblical sexual ethics are not based on the idea that bodies are worthless.
They are based on something almost infinitely more demanding:
Your body matters enormously to God.
“ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς... ἐστιν”
“Do you not know that your body is a temple...?”
Then comes the sentence our culture desperately needs:
“δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.”
Doxasate dē ton Theon en tō sōmati hymōn.
Not merely glorify God with your worship playlist.
Not merely with your Sunday attendance.
Closing the browser can become worship.
Deleting the conversation can become worship.
Refusing to sexualize the stranger can become worship.
Protecting the person you are dating can become worship.
Honoring your husband or wife can become worship.
Repenting after sexual failure can become worship.
Walking away when every nerve in your body wants to stay can become worship.
Sometimes worship sounds like a choir.
Sometimes worship sounds like a trembling person whispering at 1:17 in the morning:
And maybe that is where this article found you.
In the middle of a war.
But you are tired of fighting your body.
Promise God it was the last time.
Then find yourself kneeling beside the same bed carrying the same shame.
And eventually you begin wondering whether Jesus has become tired of you.
The Gospel does not say your sin is insignificant.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace walks directly into darkness and rescues sinners from it.
The cross does not tell us sexual sin does not matter.
The cross tells us sin mattered enough that redemption cost blood.
This is why Christianity offers something far greater than “control yourself.”
Paul's words “you were bought with a price” point beyond behavior modification.
You are not merely trying to become a slightly more disciplined version of yourself.
If you belong to Christ, you belong to the One who purchased His people at unimaginable cost.
The One calling you away from lust is the One who gave Himself to rescue sinners.
Repentance is not God standing far away shouting, “Clean yourself up before coming near Me.”
The Gospel announces that Christ receives sinners who come to Him, forgives, cleanses, transforms, and teaches them to walk differently.
So bring Him the real thing.
“Jesus, pornography owns more of me than anyone knows.”
“Jesus, I have been emotionally using someone.”
“Jesus, I keep fantasizing about someone who is not mine.”
“Jesus, I have treated my boyfriend or girlfriend like their body exists for me.”
“Jesus, I have used sex to feel loved.”
“Jesus, I let people use me because being wanted temporarily felt better than being lonely.”
“Jesus... I don't know how to stop.”
That is the person Christ came to save.
This is where scandal can become grace.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Because Jesus can write something beyond it.
Look at the people surrounding Christ in the Gospels.
The sexually broken came near Him.
The socially disgraced came near Him.
People carrying histories they could not erase discovered that their worst chapter did not have authority to write the ending.
But grace does not merely say, “You are forgiven; continue.”
Jesus forgives and calls people into new life.
Toward becoming the kind of person who can look at another human being without silently asking:
What can I get from you?
How can I honor God in the way I see you?
That transformation is desperately needed because pornography, hookup culture, secret affairs, emotional infidelity and casual sexual consumption share a terrible temptation:
They can teach us to separate pleasure from personhood.
And eventually we can become skilled at experiencing bodies while becoming increasingly incapable of truly knowing people.
Paul writes in 1 Thessalonians 4 that God's will involves sanctification, sexual holiness, and learning to live with one's body in holiness and honor rather than in uncontrolled lustful passion.
Lust asks how far it can go.
Lust looks for vulnerability to exploit.
Honor sees vulnerability and becomes protective.
And the clearest picture of love Christianity possesses is not two attractive people staring into each other's eyes.
That is why the cross demolishes our selfish definitions of love.
Christ loved at cost to Himself.
Our culture frequently asks whether someone satisfies our desires.
The Gospel teaches us to ask whether our desires are being brought under the lordship of Christ.
That does not make sexuality cold.
Within God's design, sexual intimacy is not supposed to say merely:
It belongs inside the profound covenantal reality of giving oneself faithfully to another.
Not taking somebody's vulnerability and disappearing.
And if you have already failed...
Please do not stop reading here.
Because this is where the enemy loves to twist Christian conviction into hopeless condemnation.
But “already” is not stronger than the blood of Jesus.
The Gospel is for guilty people.
If salvation were only available to people with spotless histories, there would have been no reason for a cross.
Where necessary, seek wise pastoral help and accountability.
Remove access to what repeatedly pulls you into sin.
Stop romanticizing the relationship God is telling you to leave.
Stop keeping secret doors open while praying for God to close them.
But do all of this looking toward Christ, not merely staring at your failure.
And perhaps today your first act of freedom is simply refusing to hide anymore.
You do not need to publish the details of your private struggle. You do not owe strangers your secrets.
But sometimes three honest words become the moment somebody stops fighting completely alone.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need proof that failure does not have to become destiny.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media activity.
Someone may be smiling in family photographs while pornography is quietly destroying their marriage.
Someone may be confusing being sexually desired with being genuinely loved.
Someone may believe their past has permanently disqualified them from Christ.
Someone may be one honest encounter with the Gospel away from finally saying:
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the Christian who has become lukewarm.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
Support Christian ministry because the Gospel has made you generous, because you believe the work is worth helping, and because you want sound Christian resources to continue reaching people.
If you are ready to support the mission and go deeper with us:
Jesus wants more than your money.
All of it under His gracious lordship.
Because the answer to lust is ultimately bigger than trying harder not to look.
It is learning to see people through eyes being transformed by Jesus.
The woman is not a body for your imagination.
The man is not a body for your validation.
Your spouse is not an instrument for your satisfaction.
Your boyfriend is not your possession.
Your girlfriend is not your possession.
The person on the screen is not pixels.
The person you are tempted to use bears a dignity your appetite does not have permission to erase.
You are more than what you did with your body.
More than what somebody did to your body.
More than the photograph you sent.
More than the night you regret.
At the cross, Jesus Christ demonstrates both the seriousness of sin and the staggering depth of divine mercy.
Learn how to see another human being again.
remember the Savior whose scarred hands answered with His life:
Because maybe your comment will become somebody else's courage to stop pretending.
And maybe tonight the greatest miracle will not be that your desires suddenly disappear.
Maybe the miracle will be that, for the first time in a long time, you look at another human being and see more than a body.
Someone Christ commands you to love rather than consume.
Someone whose dignity matters more than your momentary appetite.
And then you look into the mirror...
and finally understand that grace has been teaching God to you there too.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life, but it does not get to hold the pen when Jesus has taken the story.
